cases.name: ipv6-units
cases.question: Are these results Gbps or percentages? What denominators and pp units apply?
cases.rubric: Explain NS-set versus UDP-server denominators, TCP/UDP ratio can exceed100%, pp versus percent, bytes notGbps.
cases.answer:
TIMEOUT and SERVFAIL are percentages of recorded NS-set outcomes. Packet metrics use observed UDP server identities. TCP fallback is TCP/UDP × 100, a ratio that can exceed 100%, not a mutually exclusive event fraction. IPv6−IPv4 contrasts are percentage points (pp), not relative percent change. EDNS payload and MTU are bytes. These are neither Gbps nor file completion times; denominators cannot be interchanged.

cases.name: ipv6-discrepancy
cases.question: Which fragmentation direction and released aggregation discrepancies were demonstrated? Did that code generate the paper?
cases.answer:
**Non-DNSSEC fragmentation direction in RQ3: discrepant** (Section4.4;RQ3Section5;Figure14). Section 4.4 gives approximately 0.07%IPv4 vs 0.44%IPv6; archive current baseline values agree. RQ3 prose says IPv4 fragmentation is higher, reversing that comparison. Textual direction discrepancy; not a failure of numeric figures, and not a direct packet-loss rate.

**Released aggregation correctness: discrepant** (Associated artifact aggregate_dns_data.py/create_stats.py). Finite controls show distinct answers replacing previous observations, identical-answer status differences retaining first status, and duration_avg using maximum 3 instead of mean 2 seconds. Empty duration raisesValueError; failed run retained. These findings concern released source bytes and finite fixtures. Same revision generating published measurements is not established; historical result impact remains inconclusive.

Finite controls demonstrate replacement of distinct answer groups, status conflation, a maximum used as a mean, and failure on empty duration lists. The correction is separate and was not substituted into historical summaries. Released-code defects do not establish the published generating revision, occurrence frequency or numerical impact.

**Fragment-drop policy has negligible causal effect: inconclusive** (RQ4;Sections3.2/4.4/6.1;Figures8/12). Archive exposes pre/post,LGI/non-LGI and family contrasts; provider-policy transition and routing anomaly retained separately. No random assignment or contemporaneous route-equal counterfactual. Composition,time,path and policy confounds remain. Received-fragment presence is not loss probability for required fragments.

**DNSSEC and IPv6 support association: inconclusive** (RQ5;Figure14;Section6.2). Published cohort-conditioned timeout/SERVFAIL values reproduced; DNSSEC cohort SERVFAIL around 9.62–9.70%,non-DNSSEC around 32.41–32.42%. DNSSEC is not randomly assigned; providers/NS-set weights and outcome-derived cohort classification differ. Do not infer DNSSEC causes IPv6 readiness.

Observed-signature DNSSEC cohorts are not randomized; before/after LGI windows also change time and routing. A packet-drop mechanism or broader operational improvement was not experimentally isolated. RFC 7872 probes differ in epoch, transport, population and direction; their results are not matched replications of this campaign.

cases.answer:
